newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dollar caught by contrary currents.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dollar caught by contrary currents.

text.p: The Australian dollar inched lower Tuesday as a tight thirty tick trading range belied a bumpy session which saw it batted around by a variety of players.

The currency had stolen higher early on, encouraged by talk of demand linked to a dual currency samurai bond. But the rally came unstuck at US$0.7890 as a U.S. fund out of HongKong sold aggressively and a local bank dumped AUD/yen in size.

Exporter bids were enough of a cushion to keep the currency above US$0.7860 despite several more bursts of selling, possibly related to an options expiry. The net result of this messy manoeuvring was to reinforce the market's sense of stalemate.

"We've seen some good amounts go through, but always in both directions," said a dealer at a local bank. "It strongly suggests the market is divided on where the AUD goes now and could coop it up in the US$0.7855/7945 box for some time yet."
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local currency was caged at US$0.7874/79 from an early US$0.7875/80 and US$0.7886/91 late here Monday.

The dollar was also vulnerable on the crosses after fleeing to 87.49/59 yen from 87.72/82 late Monday and a four year high if 89.21 just a week ago. In trade weighted terms it slipped to 58.2 from a previous 58.4 finish.
Dollar supporters took comfort in a couple of dual currency samurai bonds from the NSW Treasury Corp which showed the Japanese had not completely lost their taste for A$ debt.
They noted one of the issues sought to counter currency risk by offering to pay principal in yen, as opposed to dollars, if the AUD/yen rate was above a certain level on expiry.

"When you have to start dressing up your products like this its usually a sign of impending saturation," said one dealer. "It implies the yield is no longer high enough by itself to attract sufficient demand."
Neither would the sudden talk of a Japanese rate rise help.
The market had been unsettled by suggestions from two Japanese politicians that interest rates there might rise after the election on October 20.
Most analysts dismissed the talk as a ploy to win votes from savers disgruntled at record low rates, and doubted the Bank of Japan would take any risks with the fragile recovery.

But more political posturing was likely and the market was very sensitive to any suggestion of higher Japanese rates given the whole world had been borrowing in yen to invest in high yielders, such as the Australian dollar.
The prospect of a domestic rate cut added further risk.
The futures market had already priced in a 0.50 point cut in official rates to 6.5 percent by December and some troublemakers were suggesting the easing process might not end there.
The 90-day bank bill contract for March 1997, for instance, had shot to 93.57 from 92.77 a month ago, implying a rate of 6.43 percent.

Some analysts believe the economy is close to turning upward and are not so sure even one rate cut is required. But they conceded the call is a close one and say much will depend on how the real side data and the quarterly inflation and wages figures turn out in the run up to the next RBA meeting on November 5.
The first key indicator will be employment for September on Thursday when economists expect a fall of around 7,500 as a modest payback for August's 37,900 rise.
Elsewhere, the Kiwi dollar remained depressed by political uncertainty ahead of the New Zealand election on October 12.

Labour leader Helen Clark, whose party has sharply narrowed the government's lead in the polls, reassured financial markets that a Labour-led government would keep the economy on track. She supported a strong NZ$, but added it was undesirable for the currency to keep on rising so fast.
